entries.title: CONTEST FOR PAINTINGS
entries.note: The only call-for-entries notice found, for the first (1957) competition. Quoted from Trove OCR with obvious OCR slips corrected: 'Entries have opened for the Maude Vizard-Wholohan art prizes competition, run by the Royal South Australian Society of Arts. Prize-money is £300 for a landscape or seascape in oils, £100 for a water-colour (any subject), and £25 for a print (any subject). Entries close on June 14. The competition is open to Australian-born artists and artists who have lived in Australia for three years before the closing date. The entries must be original and must have been done in the 18 months before June 14.' This shows a watercolour class of any subject (so a portrait qualified) and an 18-month painting window. No judges are named. Note: the full article is copyright-blocked on Trove ('still within its copyright period'); the wording was checked on 7 Nov 2026 through Trove search snippets, which show '... in oils, £100 for a [water-colour] (any subject), and £25 for a print (any subject)', '... close on June 14. The competition is open to ... artists who have lived in ...' and 'The entries must be original and must have been done ...'.

entries.title: Worth Reporting (item 'An art prize with memories')
entries.venue: Australian Women's Weekly, p. 31, via Trove
entries.note: Confirms 1957 was the first contest. Quote: 'YOUTHFUL memories were revived for well-known Australian artist Hans Heysen when he was recently awarded second prize in the first Maude Vizard-Wholohan Art Contest, held in Adelaide.' Also: 'First prize went to South Australian Louis James, now living in London, and third prize to Murray Griffin, of Victoria, a Japanese P.O.W. during World War II.' It does not say which category each prize was. It wrongly says Mrs Wholohan died in 1951 and left the money to the Royal S.A. Society of Arts. No Battarbee mention.

entries.title: Artbursts: The Hiroshima Panels (includes section 'Adelaide Shows'), by Geoffrey Dutton

entries.note: Review of the 1958 prizes, read from the page OCR (nla.obj-687016450 and nla.obj-687016718). Quote: 'The South Australian Maude Vizard-Wholohan art-competitions for an oil of figures, a watercolor and a print offer really substantial prize-money, which this year attracted many inter-State entries. The S.A. judges, with an impartiality admirable but perhaps excessive, awarded the oil prize to Clifton Pugh, of Victoria, the watercolor to Hector Gilliland, of N.S.W., and the print to another Victorian, Lesbia Thorpe.' This confirms a 1958 watercolour category. Other exhibitors named: J. Carington Smith, Charles Bush, Margarita Stipnieks, Juta Puust. Battarbee is not mentioned. Judges' names and prize amounts are not given.

entries.title: Valuable Art Prize Bequest
entries.note: Terms of the original will. Quote: 'An art prize worth £200 to be offered annually by the SA National Gallery and SA Royal Society of Arts is provided for by a substantial bequest from the estate of the late Mrs. F. Wholohan, who died on September 7, aged 91.' Also: 'Competitors must have lived in Australia for at least seven consecutive years before the date of the competition.' The subjects were to alternate each year, 'one year a portrait and the following year a landscape or seascape.' The winning picture was to become the property of the National Gallery and hang with the artist's name, 'and later to be sent to a country institute.'

entries.title: Views differ on art prize
entries.note: Quote: 'The prize will be offered annually by the SA National Gallery and the SA Royal Society of Arts.' Also: 'Included in the conditions of the prize are that the winner must have resided for at least seven consecutive years in Australia, and that the subject of the paintings shall alternate from year to year, one year a portrait, the next a landscape or seascape.' entries.title: RULING SOUGHT ON £10,000 ART GIFT

Before Mr. Justice Mayo it was revealed today that the Art Gallery Board are disclaiming the trust.' The executors were Bagot's Executor and Trustee Co. Ltd.

entries.title: Supreme Court, Civil Sittings (item 'Art Bequest In Doubt')

entries.note: Raw OCR: 'A test note on tne east name ot tne loaa Kiver, near Mr. Battarbee's residence, has proved that a suitable supply exists there'. This reads as a test hole on the east bank of the Todd River. So by April 1957 his home was on the east side of the Todd, the same side as Sturt Terrace. entries.title: Katinggura
entries.venue: Art Gallery of South Australia, Adelaide
entries.note: Watercolour on paper. Accession 20001P2. Credit: A.M. and A.R. Ragless Bequest Funds 2000. Place made: Hermannsburg, NT. The page records it as signed and dated lower right 'REX BATTARBEE _ 1938', the same signature layout as Egoota. The page does not name or describe the sitter (the title may be his name, but the page does not say so). Image URL: https://agsa-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/media/dd/images/69013-HQ-20001P2.a6caab1.jpg. I viewed the image. It is a bust-length bearded Aboriginal man in three-quarter view looking to the viewer's left, set right of centre against a big plain sky with a low horizon of rocks. That is the same compositional formula and almost the same sheet format as Egoota (38 x 50). Differences: long twisted, forked beard; hair tied up in a bun bound with a thin yellow hair-string, not a red band; pale cream sky, not blue; low pink-grey rocks and green spinifex along the bottom edge instead of a red rock face and distant hills. Lined forehead and stern sideways look are similar. In my view this is not the same man. He does look like the sitter in the 1942 'Arunta Tribal Elder' (bun, yellow string, long forked beard), which would suggest Battarbee repainted the same sitters years apart, but that is my visual impression only. Apart from Warrnambool's Munduckinera, this is the only Battarbee portrait of an Aboriginal person I found in a public collection online.

entries.title: Uncovering a legacy: a daughter's quest to track down her father's paintings
entries.note: Headline as shown when fetched (the URL slug is worded differently). Published 7:00am 15 Aug 2025, updated 10:41am the same day. A subscription prompt shows, but the fetched text ran to the end of the story. Gayle Quarmby (nee Battarbee) is asking the public to help find her father's lost paintings, especially early works from the 1920s to 1940 that she thinks may still be around the Warrnambool district. She is "penning a book about her father's life and art", with a Warrnambool launch planned later in 2025. The article puts his complete output at about 700 paintings. The only contact route given is the email quarmbyhort@gmail.com. No website, Facebook page or publisher is named. It mentions the 1956 portrait Munduckinera, Pintubi Tribesman at Warrnambool Art Gallery, describing the sitter as a first-contact Aboriginal man, and says other works are in national and private collections. There is no mention of a register, database or catalogue raisonne, or of Egoota, the Pitjantjatjara or the Maud Vizard-Wholohan prize. prize_findings: Short answer: the label fits 1958, not 1955. (1) No prize ran in 1955 or 1956. Elizabeth Maude Wholohan (nee Vizard) died 7 Sep 1950. Her 1947 will left about £10,000 to the National Gallery of SA Board for an annual £200 Maude Vizard-Wholohan Art Prize, offered with the SA (Royal) Society of Arts, subjects alternating portrait and landscape or seascape, entrants resident in Australia seven years (Advertiser 27 Sep 1950, https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/45671045; News 27 Sep 1950, https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/131223734). In Dec 1954 the Gallery Board disclaimed the trust and the executors went to the Supreme Court; counsel said 'The Society of Arts might be able to execute the trust' (News 9 Dec 1954, https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/131215673; Advertiser 10 Dec 1954, https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/47618539). July 1957 sources call that year's contest the first (Women's Weekly 31 Jul 1957 'the first Maude Vizard-Wholohan Art Contest', https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/48076456; AGSA Bulletin July 1957 'The first Maude Vizard-Wholohan award', https://www.printsandprintmaking.gov.au/references/1267/; AGSA timeline '1957: The first Maude Vizard-Wholohan Art Prize is held'). Caveat: the Adelaide dailies on Trove stop in 1954, so a small 1955-56 event can't be completely ruled out, but nothing points to one. (2) 1957 rules: run by the Royal SA Society of Arts; £300 for an oil landscape or seascape, £100 for a watercolour of any subject, £25 for a print of any subject; entries closed 14 June 1957; open to Australian-born artists and three-year residents; works original and done in the 18 months before 14 June (Telegraph, Brisbane, 16 Jan 1957, https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/294737258, full text copyright-blocked, wording checked via Trove search snippets). Results: first Louis James, second Hans Heysen, third Murray Griffin (Women's Weekly); Griffin won the £25 print prize (AGSA Bulletin); the classes of the other two aren't stated. Judges not found. (3) 1958: classes were an oil of figures, a watercolour and a print, with 'many inter-State entries'; Clifton Pugh won the oil, Hector Gilliland the watercolour, Lesbia Thorpe the print (£25) (Geoffrey Dutton, The Bulletin, 9 Jul 1958, https://trove.nla.gov.au/work/233671451; AGSA Bulletin July 1958, https://www.printsandprintmaking.gov.au/references/2077/). 1958 closing date, judges and the oil and watercolour prize money not found. (4) Catalogues: an annual 'Maude Vizard-Wholohan Art Prizes Exhibition' catalogue series is held by the Art Gallery of NSW Research Library (Trove https://trove.nla.gov.au/work/8534200, years not shown). SLSA has no 1957 or 1958 catalogue; Australian Prints + Printmaking has exhibition records only for 1959, 1960 and 1962; the AGSA Bulletin reviews are known only from abstracts; the AGSA Research Library catalogue wasn't found online. (5) Battarbee is not recorded as an entrant, hung or commended in any source found. Dutton's 1958 review names Pugh, Gilliland, Thorpe, J. Carington Smith, Charles Bush, Margarita Stipnieks and Juta Puust only. (6) Why 1958: there was no 1955 prize; the painting is dated 1957; a 1957 work fits a 1958 entry under the 18-month rule (if 1958 kept it); and Battarbee's Tmara-Mara Galleries ads first give 'STURT TERRACE' on 14 Feb 1958 (earlier ads give no street). He already lived on the east bank of the Todd, the Sturt Terrace side, by April 1957, so the address supports 1958 without proving it. The house number 6 isn't in any Trove item. Best confirmation would be the 1958 exhibition catalogue (AGNSW Research Library series or AGSA Research Library).
family_contact: Gayle Quarmby (nee Battarbee), his daughter, is asking the public to help find his lost paintings, especially early works from the 1920s to 1940 that may still be around Warrnambool (The Standard, 15 Aug 2025). The only public route for the project is the email printed in that article: quarmbyhort@gmail.com. I found no project website, Facebook page or publisher. She was writing a book on his life and art, with a Warrnambool launch planned for later in 2025. She is also named as the copyright holder on at least one NGV work. I did not contact her. The book now appears to be out. The SLSA catalogue lists 'Rex : artist & Albert Namatjira's friend / Gayle & Ken McGregor', Melbourne: Badger Editions, 2026, 296 pages, colour illustrations and portraits (https://www.catalog.slsa.sa.gov.au/search/X?SEARCH=Quarmby%20Battarbee). genuine_for: 1. An independent earlier record: Waddington's, Toronto, 17 Nov 2003, lot 25, offered two Battarbee watercolours as one lot, a ghost gum and 'EGOOTA', 'the latter dated 1957, each signed and titled verso', each about 41.4 x 51.6 cm, est. CAD 700-900 for the pair (https://www.invaluable.com/auction-lot/rex-battarbee-1893-1973-australian-ghost-gum-macd-25-c-q39i1x3jp3). Same title, same year, similar size, and 'titled verso' fits the back label. It was on the market 23 years ago at a low estimate, long before Battarbee prices rose, so there was little reason to fake it. 2. The back label fits facts a later faker would struggle to get right: the prize had a watercolour class of any subject in 1957 and 1958 for work painted in the previous 18 months, and Battarbee's own ads first give the Sturt Terrace address in Feb 1958. A 1957 painting entered in 1958 fits all of it. 3. The label's unusual spelling 'Pitjentjara' is the spelling in the catalogued title of his 1967 portrait 'Portrait of Willie Tjimba/Pitjentjara Tribe', and the 'name, tribe tribesman' title pattern matches Chingu, Pintubi Tribesman; Teltelkna, Pitjantjatjara Tribe; Nabi, Puntubi Tribesman; and 'Agar Nabi a Pintubi tribesman' (Chronicle, 29 Nov 1956). 4. The signature (REX BATTARBEE in capitals, long underline, then the year) matches Arunta Tribal Elder 1942, Chingu 1965, Study of an Aboriginal Girl 1936, and AGSA's Katinggura 1938, which AGSA records as signed 'REX BATTARBEE _ 1938'. 5. The composition is his standard portrait formula: bust-length, three-quarter view, big sky, low horizon, rock behind (Katinggura 1938 at AGSA, https://www.agsa.sa.gov.au/collection-publications/collection/works/katinggura/27727/; Arunta Tribal Elder 1942). 6. He was painting named tribesman portraits in Alice Springs in late 1956: the Chronicle (29 Nov 1956) says he 'is painting portraits' (https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/297705242). 7. In the close-up photos the paper grain shows through the paint and the signature looks painted, which fits an original watercolour rather than a print. This still needs checking in person.
genuine_against: Nothing found points against it. The gaps are: 1. No record yet that Egoota was actually entered, hung or commended. No 1958 entry list was found, and the Adelaide dailies on Trove stop in 1954. 2. The label year can be read as 1955, and no prize ran in 1955. A 1955 reading would clash with the 1957 date on the front, so it is most likely a misread 1958. 3. It isn't in any public collection found, isn't in his 1951 book (no portraits of his own there), and isn't among AASD's 205 titles. The only auction record is the 2003 Toronto lot, with no visible image or result, so that match rests on title, date and size alone. The sizes differ slightly (41.4 x 51.6 cm there, about 38 x 50 cm here), which could be sheet versus sight size. 4. It's a late work (1957) with unusually blue-violet skin tones, unlike Arunta Tribal Elder and Chingu. The 1936 Study of an Aboriginal Girl is just as blue, so this is a point to note rather than a red flag. 5. Ownership between 2003 (Toronto) and now is unknown. 6. All photos were taken through glass, so condition (foxing, fading, mat burn, tears) is unknown.
value_estimate_aud: AUD 5,000-10,000 hammer at a major Australian house (Deutscher and Hackett, Menzies, Leonard Joel, Lawsons, Smith & Singer), roughly 6,200-12,500 with premium. This is my judgement. The upside is more if two collectors chase it, as with Arunta Tribal Elder. The downside is a pass-in, as with Willie Tjimba and Chingu. Context: his landscapes have made AUD 7,500-19,000 since 2021, for example D&H AUD 10,432 inc. premium (Oct 2026) and Menzies AUD 19,000 (Aug 2026), and named portraits are rarer than landscapes. Three closest comparables: (1) Arunta Tribal Elder, 1942, 34 x 47 cm, Lawsons, 15 Aug 2024. Sold AUD 20,000 on a 5,000-7,000 estimate; ArtRecord's AUD 24,545 looks like the same sale with premium (https://www.lawsons.com.au/auction-lot/rex-battarbee-1893-1973-arunta-tribal-elder-1942-_67748a7b98). (2) Chingu, Pintubi Tribesman, 1965, 36.5 x 40.5 cm, Mossgreen, 22 Jul 2014. Sold AUD 5,500, below a 7,000-10,000 estimate, after passing in at D&H in 2008 and Elder Fine Art in 2010 (https://www.liveauctioneers.com/item/28336130_reginald-ernest-rex-battarbee-1893-1973-armadale-victoria). (3) Portrait of Willie Tjimba of the Pitjentjara Tribe, 1967, 37 x 43 cm, Colville, 20 Sep 2016. Passed in at 2,000-3,000, and also passed in at Theodore Bruce in 2003 at 500-700 (https://www.invaluable.com/auction-lot/rex-battarbee-1893-1973-portrait-of-willie-tjimba-79-c-2b74925a55). Closest in subject but unpriced: Teltelkna, Pitjantjatjara Tribe, 1946, 37.5 x 46.5 cm, Deutscher-Menzies, Mar 2005, est. 1,200-1,800, ex G.M. McKinlay, Launceston (https://www.invaluable.com/auction-lot/rex-battarbee-auction-date-17-march-2005-1893-197-470-c-36p33und1b).
still_to_check: Before Wednesday: 1. Inspect it in person, out of the glare and ideally out of the frame. Check for paper texture, brush marks and a painted (not printed) signature. Check condition: foxing, fading, mat burn, tears. Look for any other labels or stickers on the back; a Waddington's lot sticker or a Canadian framer's label would tie it to the 2003 Toronto sale. Measure the sheet (Waddington's gave about 41.4 x 51.6 cm). 2. Ask the auction house where it came from, and its buyer's premium rate. Then set a hard ceiling that includes the premium. 3. Decide whether it's a keeper or a resale. At a major house, selling costs and pass-in risk eat a lot of the gap. After the sale: 4. Look at the new family book 'Rex: artist & Albert Namatjira's friend' (Badger Editions, 2026, 296 pp, colour illustrations and portraits) for Egoota or the same sitter. Wait until after the sale before sending Gayle Quarmby photos, so the family doesn't become an underbidder. 5. The 1958 Vizard-Wholohan catalogue (AGNSW Research Library series, or the AGSA Research Library), to confirm whether Egoota was hung. 6. Waddington's (Toronto) for the 2003 image and result. 7. SA Museum Archives AA 662/103 'Sales from Battarbee ... lists of paintings'. 8. Whether the 1940 'Nabi, Puntubi Tribesman' (AIATSIS photo, https://trove.nla.gov.au/work/246784145) or the 1956 'Agar Nabi' shows the same man.

identification: A decorative Kunstkammer-style 'Prunkstillleben', a pastiche of 17th-century Dutch and German still lifes, signed roughly 'Aug. Scholz'. entries.title: Artist search: no painter called August (or A.) Scholz traced
entries.note: Artist: Not found. No painter called August (or A.) Scholz turned up in any source I could reach. The only 'August Scholz' with a record is a writer and translator (1857-1923, born Imielin, died Berlin; Deutsche Biographie index, GND 115373853, variants 'Scholz, A.' and 'Scholz, Aug.'; https://deutsche-biographie.de/sfzS08386.html). 'Augustin Scholz' is a Catholic theologian (1794-1852, Kapsdorf-Bonn; https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz78919.html). The painter namesakes I found are Werner Scholz (1898-1982, Berlin-Schwaz, expressionist; GND 118759051), Georg Scholz (1890-1945, New Objectivity), Richard Scholz (German, 1860-c.1938, Munich; University of Vienna DoME database), Paul Scholz (1859-1940; a 1927 landscape signed 'P.Scholz, 27'; Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek/Foto Marburg) and Wilhelm Scholz (1824-1893, Berlin draughtsman, painter and caricaturist; ULB Düsseldorf). None of them is a still-life specialist and none signs 'Aug.'. Search results showed Invaluable pages for Werner and Martin Scholz and Van Ham lots for Werner and Richard Scholz, but nothing for an August Scholz on Invaluable, Van Ham, Lempertz, Neumeister, Hampel, Lot-tissimo or Bassenge. I didn't check login-only databases (artnet, Arcadja, askART, AKL). Signature: No comparison was possible because I found no signed work by an August or A. Scholz. The only namesake signature I saw recorded is Paul Scholz's 'P.Scholz, 27', and that initial doesn't fit. In the photos, the signature is small and cursive, in dark brown paint on the red tablecloth at lower right, just under the lace border. The surname reads as 'Scholz', though at this resolution 'Schulz' can't be ruled out. The first name is a short abbreviation that could be 'Aug.' but isn't clearly legible. I can't see a date. The photos don't show whether the signature went on at the same time as the paint. On the rest of the picture: the handling is competent but fairly flat and decorative. The red cloth is done in streaky vertical strokes and the lace is dabbed in. The open book has scribbled pseudo-text. On the wall is a Dutch windmill landscape. The black lacquer cabinet has two painted roundels with figure scenes and gilt arabesque panels. There's a gilt-mounted nautilus cup with a lid and finial, a blue charger with a dark pattern, a jade-green crouching animal figure on a plinth, and a red-mottled vase of white and blue flowers. The stone tablet has a large ornamental initial and four lines of pseudo-Gothic lettering, partly covered by lace. The frame is wide and ebonised, with deep leaf ornament and a gilt slip. Nothing in the photos suggests an old-master or high-end hand. Inscription: Only line 2 is clearly legible: 'herr MARKGRAF ALBERT', with one or two more letters hidden under the lace (possibly 'ALBERTU[S]'). The other three lines can't be read reliably in these photos. I can make out only fragments, something like 'hier ba..' on line 3, and '..allein' and maybe '..hülf' on line 4. The rest of this is from general historical knowledge and wasn't checked online this session. 'Markgraf Albrecht/Albert' points most naturally to the Hohenzollern margraves of Brandenburg. Candidates are Albrecht the Bear (c.1100-1170, first Margrave of Brandenburg), Albrecht Achilles (1414-1486), Cardinal Albrecht of Brandenburg (1490-1545, the Renaissance art patron and collector), Albrecht of Brandenburg-Ansbach (1490-1568, first Duke in Prussia, Latin 'Albertus', after whom Königsberg's Albertina university was named) and Albrecht Alcibiades of Brandenburg-Kulmbach (1522-1557). The legible fragment doesn't say which. The layout looks like a 16th-century dedication or building plaque, a standard prop in 'Altdeutsch' historicist still lifes. The modern spelling 'MARKGRAF' in Roman capitals and 'Albert' rather than 'Albrecht' suggest the painter invented or modernised it rather than copying a real 1500s tablet. So it suggests a German-speaking painter working in the neo-Renaissance taste, which ran from the 1870s well into the 20th century. It doesn't narrow the date further.

value_estimate_aud: Bid on it only as a decorative picture you like, not as a find. On this evidence I'd put fair auction value at roughly A$150 to A$500, and a good part of that is the heavy ebonised frame. That range is my judgement from the comparables, not a quoted figure. Why: (1) No painter called August Scholz shows up in any reference or auction source I could reach, so there's no name premium. (2) Recognised names in this exact genre do sell. Schäffer's nautilus cup and grapes (58.5 x 48 cm) made EUR 3,096 with premium at Van Ham in 2017, and a Zatzka Prunkstillleben made EUR 5,160 with premium in 2019. That's the name talking. (3) The fairer comparison is minor German painters doing the same nautilus-cup set-ups, such as Huber-Andorf (1877-1965). His larger canvases get estimates of only about EUR 140 to EUR 600 at German regional houses, and one was apparently re-offered lower after not selling. That's very roughly A$250 to A$1,000 at A$1.7-1.8 to the euro, a rate I haven't checked, for bigger pictures by a painter who at least has a record. (4) Even Czernotzky, a known Vienna specialist, is mostly estimated at EUR 350 to EUR 1,500. In Australia, Leonard Joel estimated his large nautilus canvas at $2,000-4,000 in 2024 and Mossgreen a small one at $600-800 in 2017, and neither result is visible. Bidding guide: if you want it on the wall, a hammer of A$300 to A$400 before buyer's premium is sensible. Above about A$600 you'd be paying for a name nobody has recorded. The upside case is if the back shows a genuine 19th-century canvas laid down, with a German colourman's stamp or old labels, and the frame turns out to be carved timber rather than moulded composition. That could justify the top of the range or a bit more, but I found nothing to suggest a sleeper.
still_to_check: (1) Turn it over. Commercial canvas board or a modern board points to the 20th century. An old canvas laid onto board, a German colourman's stamp, dealer or exhibition labels or an inscription could date it or name the painter. (2) Confirm it's oil paint and not an oleograph, an embossed print on canvas that's common in heavy frames of this era. In raking light, look for brushstrokes that follow the forms, and check that the signature and tablet lettering sit on top as paint. (3) Get a sharp close-up of the signature and the full tablet text. If the inscription turns out to be a real quotation, it could point to a source or region. (4) Frame: carved timber or moulded composition, and any losses to the ornament. (5) Condition: canvas laid on board can hide tears, flaking or overpaint. (6) Leads I couldn't open: an eBay.de listing (item 376288183992) that came up twice in 'August Scholz' still-life searches; a Neumeister lot titled 'Ludwig Adam Kunz - Prunkstillleben mit Nautiluspokal und Hummer', which looks like a good category comparison; and the Dorotheum Endre Kiss lot page. (7) Login-only sources: the artnet price database, Arcadja, askART, and AKL or Thieme-Becker under 'Scholz, August'. The realised prices for the Czernotzky and Huber-Andorf lots are also behind the Invaluable login. (8) The buyer's premium rate and GST, so the ceiling is set all-in.

(2) The closest print analogue is 'Clunes, Victoria', a colour lithograph 43 x 69 cm 'signed and titled on margin'. It has the same naming style and nearly the same size, so a matching 'Elmore, Victoria' reproduction is plausible but unproven. Jack's offset reproductions usually show the painted signature printed in the image plus a pencil signature, title and edition number in the white margin below (e.g. Mt Egerton, ed. 181/200). (3) From the photos, the signature is inside the image at lower right, which happens on both originals and reproductions. The image is a crisp, straight-edged rectangle with about 1 cm of plain paper showing between its edge and the mat bevel on every side. Pixel sampling confirms the strip at the top and bottom. Framers usually present a print this way, but a watercolour painted to a taped edge looks the same. Any pencil signature or edition number would sit under the mat. The photos are 800 x 600 px and taken through glass, so no dot screen, paper texture, pencil underdrawing, cockling or blind stamp can be seen. A plate mark wouldn't be expected on either an offset print or a watercolour. (4) Size doesn't decide it. Jack painted originals in this format (Candelo, watercolour 47 x 78), and his prints come in similar sizes (Clunes 43 x 69, Farina 45 x 70, Mt Egerton 46 x 63). Treat the medium as unknown until it's checked with a loupe.

value_estimate_aud: If it's a print: AUD 50-250 at auction, and often no sale at all. Jack reproductions this size mostly pass in or sell at low estimates. Mt Egerton (offset, 46 x 63) passed at 80-120, then again at 40-60. Moonrise at Beechworth (offset) passed at 100-200. Clunes, Victoria (43 x 69) passed at 200-400, then sold against a 100-300 estimate. A signed 1982 collotype passed at 60-120. Private and dealer asking prices run 95-395, but prints don't sell at those prices. At a AUD 400 opening bid, a print is already overpriced. If it's an original watercolour: about AUD 1,000-2,000 hammer, possibly 2,500 in a strong room. Derby, Tasmania (47 x 68, 1986) made AUD 1,600 in Oct 2026 against a 2,000-4,000 estimate. Candelo (47 x 78, the closest format and also a town scene) sold at Lawsons in June 2024 against 1,500-2,500 (price hidden). A much bigger 72 x 106 mixed media made 3,600 at Leonard Joel in March 2026. The market is soft. Many 2026 Jack originals passed in: Millthorpe twice (at 1,500-2,500 and 1,000-2,000), Lake Moondara at 800-1,200, Fishermans Cottages Bermagui at 1,300-1,500. Half-sheet originals (about 36 x 55) are estimated at 300-800. So if it checks out as an original, 400 to open is good value. Expect buyer's premium on top of the hammer.
still_to_check: 1) Before bidding past the print range, look in person with a 10x loupe or phone macro on the sky, the grass and the signature. A regular grid of tiny coloured dots means offset print. Fine random speckle with no surface relief suggests giclee. Pooled pigment, granulation, hard wash edges and pencil underdrawing mean a real watercolour. 2) Look across the surface at a low angle. A watercolour usually shows paper texture and slight cockling, while a print has a flat, even sheen. Check for fading or foxing too. 3) Ask the auction house what medium they list. Ask them to check the back for a gallery, framer or publisher label, a certificate, or a handwritten title and date. Also ask whether a pencil signature or edition number shows in the margin if the mat is lifted. 4) Confirm whether 42 x 77 cm is the image, sight or frame size, and get the buyer's premium rate. 5) Gaps in this research: the AASD price database and Lawsons' archive couldn't be read (site error or robots block).
